Name: The green screen
Definition: A wall (and often a floor) painted or draped in an even green, lit flat, so that a switcher or software can remove the green (chroma keying) and place the person in front of it over another picture.
Description:
The LL's green screen stage is in the main studio [1][2]. From the record:

- **SLAVIC/TDM 121, spring 2024:** students "posed in ballet movements" on the green screen stage and computer vision fed their poses to Stable Diffusion, so "their own bodies acted as controllers for AI art" [1].
- **AFVS 173F, spring 2025:** some students "embodied plant movements on a green-screen stage" [1].
- **TDM 119B, spring 2025:** a "full-body long shot on our green screen stage", with generative-AI backdrops "that responded to the tone and content of each piece" [1].
- **HUM 2, Oct 21, 2025:** the checklist sets "usual chromas on 1 and 2 / lumas on 3 and 4" and makes paper dolls from green screen footage [3][2].
- **The puppetry residency for TDM 129B** (April 8–10; year not given): "green screen layering" as one of the studio mechanics the LLUFs documented [4].

Marlon, Nov 17, 07:26 (voice agent's record): "the green screen (and green paper) — chroma keying — is literally the way we connect and layer multiple video feeds" [5].
HowTo:
1. Light the green evenly and keep the subject a few feet in front of it, so no shadow falls on it. (Common practice; the record does not give distances.)
2. Route the camera to a switcher input with a chroma key (HUM 2: inputs 1 and 2) [3], or key it in software: OBS's Chroma Key filter "Removes any instances of a given color from the Source ... Use this filter for green screens" [6].
3. Choose the background: a still, a video, a generated image (TDM 119B) [1] or another camera.
4. For paper dolls: shoot the person, pick a still, cut it out, adjust the color ("pull greens down"), print "on thick" [2].

What goes wrong: green clothing or props key out with the wall; green spill on the subject needs pulling down in color [2].
WhyTo:
From the record: to put students' own bodies into the image they are studying or making (SLAVIC/TDM 121, AFVS 173F) [1], and to compare how framing and setting change a performance (TDM 119B: "how technical framing influences both perception and presence") [1]. Marlon on green's place in the studio's color scheme: "So green plays a role to connect, overlay, layer things" [5].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** the green screen's lead use in an entry for faculty.

1. Putting the speaker in the source (a scholar in front of the archive, map or artwork they discuss).
2. The body as input (pose and movement driving an image or a game).
3. Many settings for one performance (the TDM 119B comparison).
HomeGameClassroom: The table-size version is [green paper](green-paper.md) under a phone. A green sheet or cloth on a wall works for a person, with a laptop running a keyer. (We suggest this; not tested by the LL.)
HomeGameDigital: OBS keys any camera feed for free [6]; most video-call apps blur or replace a background without any green at all, at lower quality at the edges. (Common knowledge; not checked against a vendor page here.)

TheLLHas: Nothing to buy: the library loads from a CDN and the models from Google at first run. The LL's own pages that use it: face paint in mk-realtime-prototypes (Sept 25 to 29), the hackathon launchers in mk-audio-editing (Oct 22), the fellows' instruments (Nov 10), the week 10 class app's /track pages (Nov 11), and the week 11 prototype /proto/hybrid/the-room-is-the-board (Nov 15).
Name: MediaPipe
Definition: A free Google library of models that run in the browser and find things in a camera's picture: the 21 points of each hand, the 33 points of each body, the 478 points of each face. A web page turns those points into moves, so a hand, a body or a face becomes the input to a game or a performance [1][2][3][4].
Description:
Google's description: "Run vision, text, audio, retrieval, and decision models directly in your app across Web, Android, iOS, Python, and Flutter" [1]. The LL uses its web version, the `@mediapipe/tasks-vision` package, through three of its models:

- **Hand Landmarker:** "21 3D keypoints per hand", with which hand it is; one hand by default, more if asked (`numHands`) [2].
- **Pose Landmarker:** "33 body landmark locations" for "each detected person", up to `numPoses` people [3].
- **Face Landmarker:** "478 3D facial landmarks per face", and, if switched on, "52 facial expression coefficients" such as `jawOpen` [4].

Marlon on why it counts here, Nov 17, 10:47, in EL's pane: "maybe coding frameworks are technologies too? like mediapipe for instance which allows pose-based input through webcam . . . I'd say this is a technology, and then you think of specific motion-to-result relations/dynamics as mechanics?" [10]. So this page is the tool; raising a hand to fire a cue, stepping into a zone to start a sound, and the rest are mechanics (see Related).

What the LL has done with it, from the record:

- **Face paint, Sept 25 to 29** (mk-realtime-prototypes): "a texture painted on the canonical face unwrap, mapped onto the live MediaPipe face mesh with three.js" [8]. Marlon's, with agents [5].
- **The hackathon launchers, Oct 22** (mk-audio-editing): MediaPipe gestures fire clips, a synth and MIDI notes; pose and motion bring loops in and out of an Eno-style live score [5].
- **The fellows' instruments, Nov 10.** Marlon's recap that day: "The LLUFs made a number of MediaPipe-related instruments, trackers, and launchers" [5]. Five were ported into the class app: hand drums, finger sound pads, a gesture-run camera, Air Band (up to five people playing in front of one webcam) and face-and-fingertip shader trails. The only footage is two minutes of four people playing Air Band, Nov 10, 16:29 [5].
- **TDM 155AI, Nov 11.** Marlon, Nov 13: "I led them through a series of live interaction kind of components, things where we would use MediaPipe to track the positions of their hands or their heads or their fingers, and then turn that into different sorts of output, whether it would be sound, or we did filter sweeps, or colors or shaders or three.js animations" [6]. Which of the prepared `/track` pages ran in class is not recorded; the inventory marks them "likely in class (inferred from Marlon's recap, unconfirmed)" [5].
- **The room is the board, Nov 15** (`/proto/hybrid/the-room-is-the-board`): the pose model tracks up to six people standing on the floor in front of a projector. Its page says it was tested with Chrome's fake camera, "Not yet tested with people in front of a real camera" [9].
HowTo:
1. **A laptop with a webcam, in Chrome,** served at `localhost` or HTTPS (the camera needs one or the other) [9]. See [Webcam](webcam.md).
2. **The network at first load.** The LL's pages load the library from jsdelivr and the model files from Google, pinned to `@mediapipe/tasks-vision` 1.1.1, the version the theremin pages use [9]. "A venue without Wi-Fi, or a slow one, breaks the camera and voice pages" [7].
3. **Start from a page that already works.** In the week 10 class app, `/track/hello` is the smallest (about 90 lines) and `/track/inputs` checks that the camera finds hands, head and body [5].
4. **One move per gesture.** A held gesture should fire once and re-arm after release (hysteresis), as the week 10 zones and the hackathon launcher do [5].
5. **Light and frame.** Even light on the hands; for bodies, the camera at chest height or higher so it sees feet [9].

What goes wrong, from the record: no models without the network [7]; graphics pages driven by it "grew glitchy" on long runs and were reset every 45 seconds for class [5]; and "This is the third or fourth time hand tracking has been rebuilt", which is why the hardening notes propose a `mediapipe-instruments` kit [7].
WhyTo:
From Marlon: pose-based input through a webcam, with the motion-to-result relation as the mechanic (Nov 17) [10]; and in class, hands, heads and fingers turned into "sound, or ... filter sweeps, or colors or shaders or three.js animations" (Nov 13) [6].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** what MediaPipe is for outside a performance.

1. The class votes or answers with raised hands, counted by the camera and shown on the studio screen.
2. A lesson in what a machine sees: the points drawn over the picture, and what the model can and cannot know about a body.
3. Movement as evidence: a gesture or pose held, timed and logged, as a step in a lab or a rehearsal.
HomeGameClassroom: Any laptop with a webcam and Chrome, online, on the room's projector [5][7]. A person who watches and plays the sounds is the paper version, and shows what the software does.
HomeGameDigital:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. Students open the one-file `/track/hello` on their own laptops and change one mapping.
2. Each student at home in front of their own webcam, their points sent to one shared screen (not built).

Definition: Near-field communication tags are small passive chips with an antenna, sold as stickers or cards, that a phone powers and reads when it touches them. Written with a web address (an NDEF URI record), a tag makes any modern phone that touches it offer to open that page [1].
Description:
What the tags are, from the week's research (sources opened by a research subagent, Nov 16) [1]:

- **Phones read them without an app.** "iPhone XS and later support background tag reading": the iPhone shows a notification, and tapping it opens an http or https link in Safari. Android phones with NFC on send a URL tag to the browser; Android 16 opens it directly, and Android 17 first shows an "open link" notification.
- **The chips.** NXP's NTAG213, 215 and 216 hold 144, 504 or 888 bytes for data. They can mirror the chip's unique ID and a read counter into the URL, which makes each tap's address different, but that is "plain ASCII, not signed": anyone who reads one URL can forge others. NTAG 424 DNA adds AES-signed messages for taps that must be proven.
- **Web NFC** (reading tags inside a web page) works only in Chrome on Android, over HTTPS.

What the LL has done with them, from the record:

- **Nov 16, evening.** The voice agent's record: "the NTAG215 cards work (nfc.cool writes them; NFC Tools didn't). A plain URL on a tag always shows iOS's 'open in Safari' banner first" [2]. Also from that night: "iPhone reads at the top edge of the back (lay cards flat and dip the top of the phone onto them); stacked cards interfere" [2].
- **Nov 17, 05:14.** "MK did get the NFC cards. Assigning them with a phone is a little quirky, but not impossible; definitely doable" [2].
- **The first proof of concept, proposed Nov 17, 06:01:** "a card for each position around the table, people tapping their phones there and then seeing whatever the secret information is on their phone" [2]. For TDM 155AI on Wednesday, designing a game with the tags "will be one of the options for people" (06:02) [2].
- **The idea behind it, Nov 16, 17:31 to 17:34:** the physical card is the game object, "its properties live digitally", and "the tap is how you update state" [3].
- **A prototype that can use a reader:** *Every tap is a row* (`/proto/hybrid/every-tap-is-a-row`, Nov 15) logs every tap; with a USB reader, a sticker can be taught to stand for a badge or a part [4]. It runs on keys and clicks without one.
- **The tabletop build, planned Nov 16:** "one table, 8 to 12 cards, 2 to 4 phones on the same Wi-Fi; join, tap a card ... see it as that player sees it, act, watch the table screen change". The plan was written but "Not launched: it waits on Marlon's go" [5].
HowTo:
From the record:

1. **Write the tags with a phone app.** On Nov 16 nfc.cool wrote the NTAG215 cards and NFC Tools did not [2]. Write one URL per tag, of the form `http(s)://<host>/tap/<tag-id>` [1].
2. **Point the URL somewhere every phone can reach.** A deployed site, or the laptop on the same Wi-Fi: `next dev` listens on all interfaces, so phones reach `http://<laptop-LAN-IP>:3111/...`, and the LAN host must be added to Next's `allowedDevOrigins` in development [1]. Write an IP, not a `.local` name, on a tag [1].
3. **Tap.** Lay cards flat and "dip the top of the phone onto them" [2]. The phone must be unlocked and in use [1].
4. **Lock last, if at all.** Locking a tag is permanent; "lock only after the URL (and host) is final, which a laptop LAN IP is not" [1].

What goes wrong, from the record:

- **The iPhone banner.** Every tag tap on an iPhone shows a notification first, so a tap is two touches [1][2]. The 18:12 post lists three ways past it: Shortcuts automations (each tag registered by hand on every phone), App Clips or Universal Links (still a confirmation card), or a native app with a persistent Core NFC session, possibly "a thin shell" around the web app [2].
- **Stacked cards interfere** [2].
- **A typo is a security hole.** "a 'vercell.app' typo on a tag led to a typosquatted scareware page ('your iPhone has been hacked')" [2].
- **A URL is not proof of a tap:** anyone can copy and load it [1].
WhyTo:
From Marlon's direction (voice agent's record):

- **Asymmetrical information at the table.** "the dealing of a hand, or something that's metaphorically a hand — the starting coordinates of some kind of game, your identity in a playful guessing game, your teammates — a revealing of asymmetrical information" (Nov 17, 06:01) [2]. He notes "Clearly this could just be done with phones" with codes, Jackbox-style; the card at each seat is the proof of concept [2].
- **A physical object with a digital side.** The card as game object whose properties (prices, hit points, history) change in play, and the tap as the move (Nov 16) [3]. He also asked where tapping "feels natural and pleasing, as opposed to clumsy and annoying" [3].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** beyond games, what a tap is for in teaching or presenting.

1. Check-in and grouping: a tag at each table or station; the tap records who is where and deals a role or a prompt.
2. Handouts that open: a tag on a printed card or poster opens its fuller digital text, the "abbreviated print, fuller digital" pattern of this week's cards without QR codes.
3. A presenter's deck in objects: each tag on the table cues the next slide or clip on the studio screen.

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. Deployed site plus printed tagged cards, sent to the instructor in an envelope.
2. QR codes printed on the same cards as the no-NFC fallback, for phones without NFC or with it off.
HomeGameDigital: Without tags, each player opens a link or enters a code on their phone, the Jackbox-style pattern Marlon names [2]; the "secret on your phone" works the same without the tap.
